title: ORDER BY Clause
description: Learn how to sort the result set of a query by one or more columns in ascending or descending order using the ORDER BY clause.

data.alt: SQL Server ORDER BY - sort by one column

data.text: The ORDER BY clause is an optional clause of the SELECT statement. It allows you to sort the result set of a query by one or more columns.

data.title: ORDER BY Syntax
data.content: Sort result set by one or more columns with optional ASC or DESC.
data.code:
SELECT
    select_list
FROM
    table_name
ORDER BY
    column_name | expression [ASC | DESC];

items: Specify a column name or an expression you want to sort in the ORDER BY clause.
If you use multiple columns, the ORDER BY clause sorts rows by the first column first, then sorts the sorted rows by the second column, and so on.
The columns in the ORDER BY clause must match either a column in the select list or columns defined in the table specified in the FROM clause.
Specify the sort order by using either the ASC or DESC keyword.

data.text: The ASC keyword sorts rows from low to high, while the DESC keyword sorts the rows from high to low. Both ASC and DESC are optional. If you do not explicitly specify either ASC or DESC, the ORDER BY clause defaults to ASC.

data.title: NULL in ORDER BY
data.text: SQL Server treats NULL as the lowest value. This means that it will place NULL before other values after sorting.

data.title: Processing Order
data.text: When processing the SELECT statement that has an ORDER BY clause, SQL Server processes the ORDER BY clause last.

data.title: Sort by One Column (Ascending)
data.content: Sort customers by first name in ascending order (default).
data.code:
SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    first_name;

data.title: Sort by One Column (Descending)
data.content: Sort customers by first name in descending order.
data.code:
SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    first_name DESC;

data.title: Sort by City then First Name
data.content: Sort by city first, then by first name within each city.
data.code:
SELECT
    city,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    city,
    first_name;

data.title: Sort by Multiple Columns in Different Orders
data.content: Sort by city descending, then by first name ascending.
data.code:
SELECT
    city,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    city DESC,
    first_name ASC;

data.text: Sort by Column Not in Select List
SQL Server allows you to sort a result set by columns specified in the table, even if those columns do not appear in the select list.

data.title: Sort by Hidden Column
data.content: Sort by state even though it is not in the SELECT list.
data.code:
SELECT
    city,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    state;

data.title: Note
data.text: The state column must be defined in the customers table. If it isn't, the query will be invalid.

data.title: Sort by First Name Length
data.content: Use the LEN() function to sort by the length of first names descending.
data.code:
SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    LEN(first_name) DESC;

data.text: SQL Server allows you to sort the result set based on the ordinal positions of columns that appear in the select list. You can use numbers like 1, 2 to reference columns by their position:

data.title: Sort by Column Ordinal Positions
data.content: 1 refers to first_name, 2 refers to last_name.
data.code:
SELECT
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
ORDER BY
    1,
    2;

data.title: Warning
data.text: Using ordinal positions in the ORDER BY clause is not recommended. Columns should be referenced by names, and if you modify the select list, you might forget to update the ORDER BY clause.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use ORDER BY to sort the result set in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order.
ASC is the default sort order.
Sort by multiple columns by specifying them in order.
Columns in ORDER BY can be from the select list or the table definition.
Avoid using ordinal positions; always use column names explicitly.
